name: Pictish
confidence_why: Rhys 2015, the one specialist study that addresses the question, states outright that the position of the Pictish accent cannot be established because every witness was filtered through Gaelic, Scots or Latin, and the single hint he raises (the loanword monadh) he himself declines to rely on, while Forsyth 1997 says nothing about stress and no source proposes a placement.

catalog_quote: We have no good or conclusive evidence for the position of the accent in Pictish (but see below). Indeed, it has not yet been ascertained where the accent was in Northern Brittonic. ... The position of the stress accent in Pictish cannot be established with any confidence, as the available evidence provides no unambiguous indications of its location. All the evidence, apart perhaps from some inscriptions, has been mediated in some way through at least one language, often more. ... Similarly place-names (apart from a scattering in Irish, Old English and Welsh documents) have been mediated by Gaelic and Scots/English, both languages with initial stress, meaning that Pictish stress-patterns in modern reflexes of Pictish items may have been modified. new_statements.rule_in_words: The author states that the position of word stress in Pictish cannot be determined: all evidence (king-lists, place-names, loanwords) has passed through initial-stress languages (Gaelic, Scots/English). One loanword, Gaelic monadh, whose /j/ > /ð/ change is accent-conditioned, tentatively suggests penultimate stress on the pre-apocope form (as in Brittonic); fn. 665 notes that after Pictish apocope this syllable would be final, and whether stress later shifted to the penult is uninvestigated.
new_statements.exceptions: Koch's derivation of Itharnan from *isarno- would require initial stress in Roman-period 'Pictish', but the author rejects that etymology (derives the name from Latin Aeternus), so it is not counted as evidence.
new_statements.domain_note: Extinct language known only from names (king-lists, place-names, ogham inscriptions) and a few loanwords into Gaelic; the statement concerns the word accent of Pictish as reconstructed from these, and the author deliberately leaves the accent unmarked throughout the thesis. The tentative penult hint refers to the pre-apocope stage.
new_statements.identity_note: The source treats Pictish (pict1238) as the language of the medieval Pictish name evidence and discusses separately a putative Roman-period 'Pritenic' stage; the accent statement covers Pictish proper and no differently named variety. The Glottolog 'grammar/phonology' count is 0; the language is extinct and known only from onomastic and inscriptional fragments.

sources.note: Section 'The Accent' (pp. 28-30): no good or conclusive evidence for the position of the accent in Pictish; it 'cannot be established with any confidence'; the Gaelic loanword monadh (/moˈnijo-/ > /moˈnið/, /j/>/ð/ only after the accent) hints that stress lay on the penult as in Brittonic, with caution; fn. 665 (p. 329) adds that after Pictish apocope the accent would then lie on the final syllable and that any later shift to the penult is uninvestigated; accent deliberately left unmarked in the thesis.
